lessons.title: Evergrande and the Collapse of China's Property Machine

body.text: China's property boom ran on a simple machine: sell homes before building them, use the cash to buy more land, and borrow the rest. The machine worked only while prices rose and buyers kept paying upfront. When Beijing cut the borrowing, it ran in reverse.

children.text: On 29 January 2024, a Hong Kong court ordered China Evergrande Group to be liquidated. It had once been China's top-selling property developer, with more than $300 billion in liabilities, making it the most indebted developer in the world. Two months later, China's securities regulator said Evergrande had inflated its revenue by 564 billion yuan, about $78 billion, across 2019 and 2020. In August 2025, its shares were removed from the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.

Evergrande was not a lone failure. It was the most visible part of a property crisis that has dragged on China's economy for years. This lesson explains how the machine worked, why it broke, and what Indian homebuyers and investors can learn from it.

body.caption: China's property crisis on the five-stage map

cells: Two decades of rising prices; developers borrow heavily and fund construction with buyers' pre-sale payments
In August 2020, regulators impose the "three red lines" limits on developer borrowing
Evergrande defaults in 2021; buyers stop buying, homeowners boycott mortgages on unfinished flats, and Country Garden defaults in 2023

children.text: Build-up: How the Property Machine Worked
Chinese developers relied heavily on
pre-sales
. A buyer paid for a flat, often taking a mortgage right away, and might not receive the keys for two or three years. That upfront cash became the developer's cheapest source of funding.

markDefs.definition: Selling homes before they are built, with buyers paying a large deposit or the full price upfront, often using a mortgage that starts immediately. The developer uses the cash to fund construction and other projects.

children.text: Buy land from local governments, often at auctions with high prices.
Start construction and immediately pre-sell flats to buyers.
Use the pre-sale cash, plus bank loans and bonds, to buy more land elsewhere.
Repeat, growing faster each year as long as prices keep rising.

This machine made property the centre of China's economy. Economists Kenneth Rogoff and Yuanchen Yang estimated that real estate and related activities, from construction to steel and cement, accounted for about 29% of China's GDP, similar to Spain and Ireland before 2008.

body.text: Pre-sales hid a dangerous mismatch. Buyers had already paid for homes that did not exist yet, while developers had spent that money on land for new projects. The model was safe only if new sales kept arriving to finish old projects. It was a rollover problem, the same trap you saw with NBFCs in 2018, but with ordinary families as the lenders.

children.text: Trigger: The Three Red Lines
Beijing knew the sector was over-leveraged. In August 2020, regulators introduced the
three red lines
. The more lines a developer crossed, the less it could increase its debt.

markDefs.definition: Borrowing limits for Chinese property developers introduced in August 2020. Developers breaching more of the three thresholds faced tighter caps on how fast their debt could grow.

cells: How much of the balance sheet is funded by what the company owes
Borrowings minus cash, compared with shareholders' equity
Whether cash on hand covers debt due within a year

body.caption: Net gearing above 100% means net debt is larger than the owners' own capital.

body.title: Test a Developer Against a Red Line
body.prompt: A hypothetical developer has total borrowings of 450 billion yuan, cash of 50 billion yuan and shareholders' equity of 150 billion yuan. What is its net gearing, in %? Give your answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Net gearing = (450 - 50) ÷ 150 × 100 = 400 ÷ 150 × 100 = 266.7%. That is more than two and a half times the 100% red line. A developer like this would face a hard cap on new borrowing, so it could only keep going by selling more homes, cutting prices or selling assets, exactly as confidence was starting to fall.

children.text: The policy was designed to cool the sector slowly. Instead, it cut off the most indebted developers from fresh borrowing at the same time. They slashed prices to raise cash, which made buyers wait for further cuts, which reduced pre-sales, which starved developers of the cash they needed to finish homes.
Panic: The Machine Runs in Reverse

events.title: Three red lines introduced
events.description: Regulators cap borrowing growth for developers that breach leverage thresholds.

events.title: Evergrande warns
events.description: The developer warns it may struggle to service its debt, sending shockwaves through global markets.

events.title: Evergrande in default
events.description: Fitch Ratings declares Evergrande in restricted default after missed payments on its dollar bonds. It is one of many Chinese developers to default that year.

events.title: Mortgage boycotts spread
events.description: Homebuyers at more than 300 projects say they will stop paying mortgages on flats that developers have not finished.

events.title: Country Garden defaults
events.description: Once seen as one of the safer large developers, Country Garden is declared in default on its dollar debt after missing a payment by the 18 October deadline.

events.title: Liquidation order
events.description: A Hong Kong court orders Evergrande to be liquidated after it fails to agree a restructuring plan for its debts.

events.title: Fraud findings
events.description: China's securities regulator finds Evergrande inflated revenue by 564 billion yuan, fines the company 4.2 billion yuan, and bans founder Hui Ka Yan from securities markets for life.

events.title: Evergrande delisted
events.description: Evergrande's shares, suspended since January 2024, are removed from the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.

body.title: China's new home sales by floor area

children.text: By 2025, the value of new home sales had roughly halved from its 2021 peak, and property investment had fallen by close to 44% since the start of the decade. Official data show new home prices down about 20% from their 2021 peak, and many analysts believe the real fall is larger. Well into 2026, prices were still falling in most major cities.

body.title: Why Did Homebuyers Stop Buying?
body.question: Chinese developers cut prices sharply to raise cash in 2021 and 2022. Why did that make their problems worse rather than better?
options: Lower prices were illegal under the three red lines
Buyers expected prices to fall further and feared their pre-paid flats would never be finished, so they delayed buying, cutting off the pre-sale cash developers depended on
Banks refused to give mortgages on any cheaper flats
Price cuts made developers pay more tax
body.explanation: In a normal market, lower prices attract buyers. In a collapsing pre-sale market, falling prices and failing developers taught buyers two lessons: wait, because prices will be lower later, and do not pay upfront, because the flat may never be built. Both cut off the cash developers needed, forcing more price cuts and more unfinished projects. This is a confidence spiral, the same logic as a bank run.

body.label: When Buyers Became the Unpaid Lenders
body.value: Mortgage boycotts at more than 300 projects, July 2022
body.context: Families were paying monthly instalments on flats that were not being built. Refusing to pay was a way of pushing developers, banks and local governments to restart construction, and it showed how pre-sales had turned millions of households into lenders to developers.

children.text: The Indian Parallel: Stalled Projects and RERA

India has faced its own version of this problem. Through the 2010s, homebuyers in projects by developers such as Amrapali in the National Capital Region paid for flats that were delayed for years or never delivered. In July 2019, the Supreme Court cancelled Amrapali's RERA registration, found that homebuyers' money had been diverted, and appointed state-owned NBCC to complete the unfinished projects.

body.title: How pre-paid homebuyers are protected: China before the crisis vs India under RERA

columns.label: China's pre-sale model
points: Pre-sale cash often used for land and other projects
Buyers exposed if the developer ran out of money
Rules on the use of pre-sale funds were enforced unevenly
Rescue came project by project, after construction had stopped

columns.label: India under RERA 2016
points: 70% of money collected from buyers must go into a separate escrow account
That money can be used only for construction of that specific project
Projects must be registered with the state RERA authority
The SWAMIH fund, set up in November 2019 with ₹25,000 crore, finances stalled but viable projects

body.title: Go deeper: why RERA's 70% rule matters

children.text: Suppose a developer collects ₹100 crore from buyers for Tower A.

cells: The developer can spend it on land for Tower B and projects in another city
If the new projects struggle, Tower A may be left unfinished
At least ₹70 crore stays in Tower A's escrow account, usable only for its land and construction costs
Most of the buyers' money stays tied to their own project

children.text: RERA does not make buying under-construction property risk-free. Developers can still be delayed, run into disputes or fail. But ring-fencing buyers' money attacks the exact mechanism that turned China's pre-sales into a system-wide crisis.

body.title: Name the Funding Model
body.textWithBlank: Selling flats before they are built and using buyers' upfront payments to fund construction is called pre-___.
body.explanation: Pre-sales. They are common in both China and India, and they are only as safe as the rules controlling how the developer can use buyers' money.

body.title: Booking an Under-Construction Flat
body.scenario: Your cousin wants to book a flat in an under-construction project in Pune, with delivery promised in three years. The developer is offering a 12% discount for paying 80% of the price upfront. The project is registered on MahaRERA, but the developer has launched five new projects in two years and some earlier towers have been delayed.
body.prompt: Using the Evergrande story and India's RERA rules, what would you tell your cousin to check, and what worries you about the offer?
body.modelAnswer: What worries me: a large discount for paying most of the price upfront is a sign the developer may need cash, and paying 80% before construction progresses shifts risk onto the buyer, the exact pre-sale exposure that hurt Chinese homebuyers. Rapid expansion into five new projects while earlier towers are delayed resembles the land-buying cycle that trapped Evergrande. What to check: first, the project's MahaRERA registration page, including the promised completion date, approvals, quarterly progress updates and any complaints. Second, whether payments are linked to construction milestones rather than time, so money is paid as floors are actually built. Third, the developer's track record on delivery of earlier projects, and whether delays were explained. Fourth, whether the bank or housing finance company lending on the project has approved it, which adds a layer of scrutiny. Fifth, the developer's finances if it is listed on NSE or BSE: debt levels, cash flow and whether it depends on new launches to finance old ones. Sixth, the escrow compliance under RERA. A sensible approach is to prefer a construction-linked payment plan, even without the discount, or to consider a ready or nearly finished project where the delivery risk is much lower.

body.title: Before Paying for a Home That Is Not Built Yet
steps: Confirm the project is registered with the state RERA authority and read its latest progress updates
Prefer a construction-linked payment plan over large upfront payments, however attractive the discount
Check the developer's record on delivering earlier projects on time
Look at how many new projects the developer is launching compared with how many it is finishing
If the developer is listed, review its debt, cash flow and any rating downgrades
Keep all payment receipts and the registered agreement for sale, so you can pursue a RERA complaint if needed

points: China's developers ran on pre-sales and heavy borrowing, and real estate with related activity grew to about 29% of the economy
The three red lines introduced in August 2020 cut borrowing for the most leveraged developers, turning the growth machine into a downward spiral
Evergrande, with over $300 billion in liabilities, defaulted in 2021, was ordered liquidated in January 2024, was found to have inflated revenue by 564 billion yuan, and was delisted in August 2025
New home sales by floor area roughly halved from 1.79 billion square metres in 2021 to 881 million in 2025, and prices were still falling in 2026
India's RERA rule requiring 70% of buyers' money in a project escrow account, along with the SWAMIH fund, targets the same pre-sale risk that broke China's property machine

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment or property purchase advice. The developer exercise and the Pune flat scenario are hypothetical and do not refer to any real company or project. Figures are drawn from court, regulatory, rating agency, academic and news sources, and China's property data continue to change.
